title: What is best Ai tools for 3D game development currently?
author: Tlamir
selftext:
Hello,

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Asset packs.

I know this is the AIGameDev sub, but 3d models are... of questionable use still, at least in terms of how much work they take to utilize. If you're not worried about consumer pc specs, then it's not a problem. But otherwise you're going to need to learn how to retopologize and fix textures, which are very doable, but most people looking for AI help with 3d are looking for quick fixes and those are not something the AI will solve for you. You will have to do them yourself, even if the modeling AI can save you hours of sculpting time per piece. The closest you'll get to production ready assets are some of the smart topology features from something like Trippo, but even then they're only adequate for props, and the textures it gens usually need significant touch-up.  Smart  mesh characters usually have too wonky of topology to work well with animations, so you really have to sculpt a lower poly model yourself that CAN animate well and bake a high poly version of the genned model on top. Most of the examples you'll see on Youtube and such are people genning incredibly high poly assets (which limits topology issues and produces extremely crisp results... But are terrible for performance even if using Unreal.)

If you don't know half of what I just described, then the TLDR is: You have to learn actual modeling/texturing in order to leverage the tools to increase your productivity. Outside of using asset packs, every workflow/pipeline that utilizes AI to generate any kind of art asset requires significant work, whether 2d or 3d, in order to actually make it production ready at a level that people won't think it's slop.

replies.author: Tlamir
replies.body: Thanks for detailed answer. Issue with asset packs, game became asset flip or not coherent in design/art. Most of the videos i saw was just not usable for real work.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: For coherency, that depends entirely on the scope of the game or the style of the game. If you have a very specific style for your game (for instance Mouse P.I. or Cuphead) you're right that it's absolutely impossible to find any significant variety of assets that all fit the style consistently. On the other hand, if you're creating a realistic 3d game or a pixel game that falls into traditional expectations, it's very easy to find diverse arrays of compatible assets. If you don't have the capacity to work in the style you want, you have to either  learn how to do that, or assess whether you really need that specific style for your game, or if others will work out better. There's a reason that most game designers will tell new designers to start out with pixel, low poly, or an equivalently simple style to learn, because it allows them to utilize a lot of asset packs as the base, but edit where needed without much learning involved (easy to shift colors, move vertices, etc.. lots of room for error.)   If your game scope is reasonably contained, you can often find a single large asset pack that c over 70-80% of the needed assets, and then produce by hand the other 20-30% either by shifting existing assets or by designing them from scratch (if the style you're using is one of the aforementioned ones... A lot harder to produce 20-30% of realistic PBR assets.)
